messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 43
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 80

She was 41 when it happened. A small cut on her forearm while chopping bell peppers—nothing unusual for a chef. But three days later, she could not lift a stockpot. Her arm was hot, red, and swollen, and then the fever hit. By the time her partner drove her to the emergency room, her blood pressure was dropping. The doctors said sepsis, likely from a common skin bacterium that had found its way past her gloves. She spent eleven days in the intensive care unit, drifting in and out of ventilator sedation. She remembers fragments: a nurse’s voice telling her to squeeze a hand, the beeping of monitors that seemed to wait for her heart to stop, and the cold pressure of a platelet transfusion. She also remembers the certainty, in those foggy hours, that she was dying—and that there was no one to call for her last meal.

Now, two years later, she is 43, still a chef, still in the same relationship. But almost everything has changed.

In the kitchen she runs, she checks the thermometer on the walk-in cooler four times a shift. She inspects every new box of gloves for pinholes, even though the person who restocks them is the same supplier she has used for a decade. When a junior cook scrapes a knuckle on the edge of a sheet pan, she has to leave the line—her chest tightens, her vision narrows, and she smells that antiseptic wipe from the ICU. She stands in the dry storage room until the feeling passes, counting the bags of flour. The other staff have learned not to ask. Twice she has thrown away an entire case of raw chicken because the packaging looked "off" to her—packaging that was perfectly intact. Losing that product cost the restaurant over four hundred dollars, but she could not take the risk.

At home, she sleeps in a separate room. Not because her partner is unkind, but because she cannot stand the sound of another person’s breathing at night. It reminds her of the respirator. She has not eaten seafood in eighteen months—not after she had a nightmare where she choked on a shrimp and woke up unable to feel her own hands. Mornings are the worst. She wakes already drenched in sweat, even in winter, her heart knocking against her ribs like a pot lid on a boiling pot. Some days she takes her own temperature five, six times, until the number finally settles on 36.7°C. She knows it is irrational. She knows it will not save her. But she cannot stop.

Her partner tells her she has become brittle. She snaps at small things—a mis-set timer, a spilled glass of wine. She has stopped cooking at home entirely. The kitchen in their apartment, once her sanctuary, is now just a room with a knife block she avoids. She orders takeout or eats the staff meal at work, but only if she has seen it being prepared. If someone offers her food from a container that has been sealed, she feels a wave of nausea. She cannot trust what she cannot watch.

When she sits in the therapy room, she folds her hands on her lap and says, “I used to be a person who made food for other people. Now I think about death every time I put something in my mouth.” She laughs a little when she says it, a short, embarrassed sound. But her eyes stay flat. She checks the clock over the therapist’s shoulder twice during the session. She will not mention the nightmares, not today. But sometime in the next hour, she will excuse herself to the bathroom and run cold water over her wrists, just to make sure her skin is still the right temperature.
